episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Characters into tokens
episodes.description: Separate spelling, token categories and lexical boundaries.
topics: How a compiler translates a program
Locate the boundary of lexical analysis

chapters.title: How a compiler translates a program
Locate the boundary of lexical analysis

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Maya and Leo here. Our section today is Characters into tokens.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: separate spelling, token categories and lexical boundaries.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with how a compiler translates a program and work our way to locate the boundary of lexical analysis.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Can you walk me through how a compiler translates a program?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A compiler translates a source program into another representation while preserving the behavior required by the source language. Lexing finds tokens, parsing finds structure, and semantic analysis checks meaning before target code is produced.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Source means the program representation being translated.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: The characters total = count + 2; become tokens, then an assignment tree, then lower-level operations.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A valid token sequence alone does not guarantee a valid assignment.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to lexemes, token kinds and attributes. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A lexeme is the exact source substring. Its token kind names a category such as identifier or integer. An attribute can point to a symbol-table entry or hold the interpreted numeric value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lexeme means the exact source substring recognized as one token.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: In sum = sum + 12;, the two occurrences of sum share an identifier spelling, while 12 is an integer lexeme whose value is twelve.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Counting distinct names is different from counting token occurrences.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: At the current character position, choose the longest prefix that is a valid token. If equally long token rules match, use the language-defined rule priority. Then restart at the first unread character.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Token kind means a category such as identifier, integer or operator.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: In count >= 10, >= is one supported operator rather than > followed by =.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An identifier such as total2 stays together.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Longest match does not search past invalid characters or decide whether an expression is grammatically valid.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Move through source text one lexeme at a time and record each occurrence, kind and character span. Treat an identifier containing digits as one identifier when its first character is a letter or underscore.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Span means source positions from the first character up to, but excluding, the end position.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: In item12 = item12 + 5;, item12 occupies one token each time, not an identifier followed by a number.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain locate the boundary of lexical analysis to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Lexical analysis recognizes tokens; parsing decides whether their arrangement follows a grammar. Semantic checks then ask whether names and operations make sense in context.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: x + * 3 contains individually recognizable tokens, but the expression grammar rejects the adjacent + and * in this position.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave characters into tokens, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A compiler translates a source program into another representation while preserving the behavior required by the source language. Lexing finds tokens, parsing finds structure, and semantic analysis checks meaning before target code is produced.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lexical analysis recognizes tokens; parsing decides whether their arrangement follows a grammar. Semantic checks then ask whether names and operations make sense in context.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: You can pause here and try the Characters into tokens activities. Pick one idea and see whether you can explain it without the notes.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Grammar structure and ambiguity
episodes.description: Use explicit trees and language conventions to resolve interpretation.
topics: Practice choosing a unique expression tree
Give balanced parentheses a unique decomposition

chapters.title: Practice choosing a unique expression tree
Give balanced parentheses a unique decomposition

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, it's Maya. I've got Leo with me for Grammar structure and ambiguity.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: use explicit trees and language conventions to resolve interpretation.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with prove ambiguity with two trees and work our way to give balanced parentheses a unique decomposition.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to prove ambiguity with two trees. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A grammar is ambiguous when at least one complete token sequence has two different parse trees. A single witness is sufficient; merely having several alternatives is not.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Grammar means a finite collection of production rules describing permitted token sequences.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For E → E - E | num, 8 - 3 - 2 can mean (8 - 3) - 2 or 8 - (3 - 2), giving different values.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Trying a finite sample cannot prove an arbitrary grammar unambiguous; deciding arbitrary CFG ambiguity is undecidable.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: There's another piece to this: encode precedence and associativity.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A grammar can separate expression levels so multiplication groups before addition, and can make repeated operators group left or right according to the language. This is a language-specific design choice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Operator means a symbol such as + that combines operand values.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For 2 + 3 * 4, multiplication produces 12 before addition produces 14.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For 9 - 4 - 1, left association gives 4.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An else can match two different if statements in an ambiguous nested-if grammar. A common language convention attaches it to the nearest unmatched if. A matched/unmatched grammar can express that convention.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Terminal means an input token used literally by a production.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: In if c1 then if c2 then action1 else action2, choosing the inner or outer owner changes when action2 runs.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Use the stated precedence and associativity rules to construct one expression tree, then evaluate children before their parent. In this independent practice, check the grouping before performing the arithmetic.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Precedence means the rule that determines which operator groups more tightly.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For 12 - 5 - 2, the usual left-associative rule selects (12 - 5) - 2 = 5; the other grouping gives 9.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Subtraction is not associative: changing the grouping can change the result.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack give balanced parentheses a unique decomposition next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The grammar S → S S | ( S ) | ε allows different concatenation groupings of one balanced word. The replacement S → ( S ) S | ε uses the first matching close to select one interior and one remaining suffix.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Nonterminal means a grammar name expanded using production rules.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For ()()(), the ambiguous grammar can group the first two pairs together or the last two pairs together.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The replacement always selects the first complete pair before recursing on the suffix.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave grammar structure and ambiguity, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A grammar is ambiguous when at least one complete token sequence has two different parse trees. A single witness is sufficient; merely having several alternatives is not.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: The grammar S → S S | ( S ) | ε allows different concatenation groupings of one balanced word. The replacement S → ( S ) S | ε uses the first matching close to select one interior and one remaining suffix.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A useful next step is to revisit give balanced parentheses a unique decomposition with an example of your own. Keep it small enough to check by hand.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Prepare and trace top-down parsers
episodes.description: Transform productions and follow pending parsing obligations.
topics: Read a recursive-descent parser as a stack

chapters.title: Read a recursive-descent parser as a stack

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Welcome to CSQuest Audio. I'm Maya, here with Leo. This section is called Prepare and trace top-down parsers.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: transform productions and follow pending parsing obligations.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with eliminate direct left recursion and work our way to trace acceptance and syntax errors.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: There's another piece to this: eliminate direct left recursion.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If A → A α | β and β does not start with A, replace it with A → β R and R → α R | ε. The new tail repeats α without immediately calling A again.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Grammar means a finite collection of production rules describing permitted token sequences.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: E → E + T | T becomes E → T R and R → + T R | ε.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A recursive-descent function can now consume a T before following the tail.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Direct-recursion elimination does not automatically remove indirect recursion, ambiguity, or every LL(1) conflict.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on factor a common production prefix.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: When alternatives share a prefix, consume that prefix once and move the remaining alternatives into a new nonterminal. This postpones the choice until more input is available.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Terminal means an input token used literally by a production.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: S → a b c | a b d becomes S → a b R and R → c | d.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The parser can decide at c versus d.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Top-down parsing starts with the start symbol and expands toward the input. Bottom-up parsing starts with the input and reduces handles toward the start symbol, reversing a rightmost derivation.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Nonterminal means a grammar name expanded using production rules.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → a B and B → b, top-down gives S ⇒ a B ⇒ a b; bottom-up gives a b ⇒ a B ⇒ S.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: The parser context must justify reversing that derivation step.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A backtracking top-down parser may try one production and restore its input position when that attempt fails. A predictive parser uses lookahead and a conflict-free table to select a production without retrying.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lookahead means upcoming input token information used to choose a parser action.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If both S → a A and S → a B begin with a, one lookahead cannot select between them in the unfactored grammar.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Greedily choosing the first listed alternative is not a proof that the grammar is LL(1).

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Now for read a recursive-descent parser as a stack. What's the key distinction?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Each nonterminal can be a parsing function. Choosing a production creates calls or terminal matches, and an ε production returns without consuming input. A predictive stack makes these obligations visible.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Empty word (ε) means a sequence containing zero tokens.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: With E → T R, T → id and R → + T R | ε, id + id expands E, matches an id, then processes the tail.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An ε production is permitted only for the appropriate lookahead; it is not an unconditional escape from errors.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A parser accepts only when the whole input has been matched and its pending obligations are exhausted. A mismatch or an empty table cell identifies the first point the current parse cannot continue.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The expression grammar rejects id + + id because the second + arrives where a T beginning with id is required.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave prepare and trace top-down parsers, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If A → A α | β and β does not start with A, replace it with A → β R and R → α R | ε. The new tail repeats α without immediately calling A again.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A parser accepts only when the whole input has been matched and its pending obligations are exhausted. A mismatch or an empty table cell identifies the first point the current parse cannot continue.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We've covered a lot in prepare and trace top-down parsers. You don't have to remember every detail at once; start by trying one of the examples yourself.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: FIRST, FOLLOW and predictive tables
episodes.description: Compute fixed-point facts and choose LL(1) productions.
topics: Compute FIRST to a fixed point
Test grammar claims with table evidence

chapters.title: Compute FIRST to a fixed point
Test grammar claims with table evidence

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, I'm Maya. Leo's with me, and today's section is called FIRST, FOLLOW and predictive tables.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: compute fixed-point facts and choose LL(1) productions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with compute FIRST to a fixed point and work our way to test grammar claims with table evidence.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on compute FIRST to a fixed point.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FIRST(X) contains terminals that can begin a word derived from X, and ε if X can derive the empty word. For a sequence, continue past a symbol only when that symbol is nullable.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Grammar means a finite collection of production rules describing permitted token sequences.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → A B, A → a A | ε and B → b B | ε, FIRST(S) contains a, b and ε.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Do not stop at a nullable first nonterminal or copy ε into the result before every symbol in the sequence is nullable.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain compute FOLLOW using suffixes to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FOLLOW(A) contains terminals that can immediately follow A in a sentential form; $ marks the end after the start symbol. Copy FIRST of the suffix without ε, and copy FOLLOW of the left side if that suffix is nullable.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Terminal means an input token used literally by a production.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For S → A B with nullable B, b can follow A and so can $.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FOLLOW never contains ε.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FOLLOW describes context after a nonterminal, not characters inside its name or the start of its own expansion.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For A → α, enter the production under terminals in FIRST(α) except ε. If α is nullable, also enter it under FOLLOW(A). More than one production in a cell is an LL(1) conflict.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Nonterminal means a grammar name expanded using production rules.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The R → ε production in the expression grammar belongs in the R,$ cell; R → + T R belongs under +.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A grammar being unambiguous is necessary but not sufficient for its particular production form to be LL(1).

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Keep a stack with $ at the bottom and the start symbol on top. Match a terminal, or use the pair of top nonterminal and one lookahead token to choose a production. Push its right-hand side in reverse order.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lookahead means upcoming input token information used to choose a parser action.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For id + id, the top-of-stack symbol must be processed before the symbols beneath it.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Expanding ε pushes nothing.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We also need to talk about test grammar claims with table evidence.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Use fixed-point sets and concrete conflicting table cells to check claims about FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1). Removing common prefixes and direct recursion is useful preparation, but it is not a guarantee.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Empty word (ε) means a sequence containing zero tokens.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → a A | a B, A → b and B → c, the S,a cell contains two alternatives even though the two complete words differ.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A language may have another predictive grammar even when this particular grammar is not LL(1).

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave FIRST, FOLLOW and predictive tables, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: FIRST(X) contains terminals that can begin a word derived from X, and ε if X can derive the empty word. For a sequence, continue past a symbol only when that symbol is nullable.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Use fixed-point sets and concrete conflicting table cells to check claims about FIRST, FOLLOW and LL(1). Removing common prefixes and direct recursion is useful preparation, but it is not a guarantee.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Try explaining test grammar claims with table evidence in your own words. If you get stuck, that chapter is a good place to listen again.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Bottom-up parsing and SLR
episodes.description: Build item states and justify each shift or reduction.
topics: Use FOLLOW to obtain SLR reductions
Check whether a grammar is SLR(1)
Compare LL, LR(0) and SLR requirements

chapters.title: Use FOLLOW to obtain SLR reductions
Check whether a grammar is SLR(1)
Compare LL, LR(0) and SLR requirements

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Welcome back. Maya here, with Leo. We've reached the section called Bottom-up parsing and SLR.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: build item states and justify each shift or reduction.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with shift, reduce and recognize handles and work our way to check reductions with empty productions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain shift, reduce and recognize handles to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A shift moves the next terminal onto the parser stack. A reduction replaces a handle by its left-hand-side nonterminal, using the current state and lookahead to justify the choice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Grammar means a finite collection of production rules describing permitted token sequences.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → C C and C → c C | d, c d d reduces the inner d to C, then c C to C, then the final d to C and C C to S.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack construct LR(0) item states next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An LR item places a dot in a production to mark recognized versus expected symbols. Closure adds productions for a nonterminal after the dot; GOTO advances over one symbol then closes the destination.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Terminal means an input token used literally by a production.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: From C → c • C, closure adds C → • c C and C → • d.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: These are alternatives within one state, not consumed input.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Moving the dot is not itself a grammar derivation step; the dot describes parser progress.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: SLR uses LR(0) item states but adds a reduction A → α only under FOLLOW(A). This removes some overly broad LR(0) reductions without changing the item automaton.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Nonterminal means a grammar name expanded using production rules.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An LR(0) shift/reduce conflict can disappear under SLR when the shift token is absent from the completed production left side FOLLOW set.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: SLR still uses a global FOLLOW set and can introduce a reduction in an inappropriate local context.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Closure predicts productions that could be needed next. It expands the set of possible items until no new item is added, while GOTO represents a transition on an actual grammar symbol.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lookahead means upcoming input token information used to choose a parser action.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The initial item S′ → • S brings in S productions and then any nonterminal productions needed at their first position.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Closure does not advance the input pointer or move the dot in existing items.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's start with read an LR ACTION cell. What do we need to know?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A table cell can shift to a state, reduce by a production, accept, or be empty for error. A conflicting cell contains incompatible actions for the same state and lookahead.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Empty word (ε) means a sequence containing zero tokens.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A reduction pops one symbol/state pair per right-hand-side symbol, then consults GOTO for the left-hand-side nonterminal.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An ε reduction pops zero pairs.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: It still pushes the reduced nonterminal and a GOTO state.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Construct the LR(0) states and restrict completed-item reductions to FOLLOW. The grammar is SLR(1) exactly when the resulting ACTION cells have no conflicts.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → C C and C → c C | d, inspect every ACTION cell rather than inferring the result from the number of states.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: LL predicts a production before its right side is consumed. LR recognizes a right side before reducing. SLR retains LR(0) states while consulting one lookahead through FOLLOW sets.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The left-recursive expression grammar E → E + T | T is unsuitable for direct predictive recursion, yet can be handled by a suitable bottom-up construction.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Parser-family claims concern a grammar construction; a language can have multiple equivalent grammars with different properties.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's spend a moment on check reductions with empty productions.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An empty right-hand side completes without consuming a terminal. Its reduction depends on the current state and permitted lookahead, then follows GOTO just like a nonempty reduction.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → A b and A → a A | ε, the parser for a b must reduce A → ε before reducing a A.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Nullable does not mean skippable at every input position; an incorrect empty reduction can conceal a syntax error.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave bottom-up parsing and SLR, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A shift moves the next terminal onto the parser stack. A reduction replaces a handle by its left-hand-side nonterminal, using the current state and lookahead to justify the choice.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An empty right-hand side completes without consuming a terminal. Its reduction depends on the current state and permitted lookahead, then follows GOTO just like a nonempty reduction.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: When you try a problem on check reductions with empty productions, talk through why each step works. That's a useful check on what has clicked.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Canonical LR, LALR and lookahead
episodes.description: Preserve context, inspect merging and diagnose conflicts.
topics: Find the limitation of global FOLLOW
Attach lookahead to each LR(1) item
Merge LR(1) states into LALR cores
Compare canonical and merged state evidence

chapters.title: Find the limitation of global FOLLOW
Attach lookahead to each LR(1) item
Merge LR(1) states into LALR cores
Compare canonical and merged state evidence

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: I'm Maya, and this is CSQuest Audio. Today, Leo and I are taking on Canonical LR, LALR and lookahead.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: preserve context, inspect merging and diagnose conflicts.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with find the limitation of global FOLLOW and work our way to separate parser conflicts from ambiguity.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack find the limitation of global FOLLOW next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: SLR adds a completed A production under every token in FOLLOW(A), even when some of those tokens cannot follow this item in its actual context. This approximation can create a conflict.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Grammar means a finite collection of production rules describing permitted token sequences.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The assignment grammar S → L = R | R, L → * R | id, R → L has an SLR conflict involving =; canonical LR(1) distinguishes the contexts.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An SLR conflict does not prove the grammar ambiguous.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Now for attach lookahead to each LR(1) item. What's the key distinction?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An LR(1) item [A → α • β, a] says that a may follow the completed A in that item context. Closure derives lookahead using FIRST(β a).

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Terminal means an input token used literally by a production.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For an item expecting B followed by a terminal, the B items receive that terminal as lookahead even if FOLLOW(B) is larger globally.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The lookahead is after the completed production, not necessarily the next symbol after the dot.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Canonical LR(1) preserves item-specific lookahead through closure and transitions. A completed item reduces only under its attached lookahead, retaining distinctions that SLR loses.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Nonterminal means a grammar name expanded using production rules.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The assignment grammar can shift = after recognizing an L in one context and reduce R → L in another without the SLR conflict.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: LALR merges canonical LR(1) states having the identical LR(0) item core, unioning the lookaheads for corresponding items. This saves states but may create new reduce/reduce conflicts.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Lookahead means upcoming input token information used to choose a parser action.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A merge must match the full set of production-and-dot pairs, not just a shared completed production or a similar state name.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Merging lookaheads preserves no blanket guarantee that every LR(1) grammar remains conflict-free.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to trace a conflict-free LALR parse. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: When equal-core merging leaves every ACTION cell unambiguous, the resulting LALR parser can shift and reduce using its compact state table.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Empty word (ε) means a sequence containing zero tokens.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → C C and C → c C | d, compare canonical and merged state counts, then parse c d d using the merged table.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Never hide a conflict by taking the first action; the parse must stop when a unique action is unavailable.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Two LR(1) states may separately distinguish when A or B can reduce. Merging their equal cores unions lookaheads, so formerly separated reductions may compete on the same token.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → a A d | b A e | a B e | b B d, A → c and B → c, canonical LR(1) succeeds while equal-core LALR merging creates reduce/reduce cells.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: It does not prove that the generated language lacks a different LALR grammar.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A decision can require seeing a pair of future tokens when the first token alone is compatible with two actions. Demonstrate this with one explicit grammar before making broader LR(k) claims.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For S → a A a b and A → a | ε, after the first a, lookahead a b selects the empty A, while a a selects A → a.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: This dedicated witness is not a general LR(2) table generator or a proof about every grammar.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: How would you explain compare canonical and merged state evidence to someone meeting it for the first time?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Count canonical states, group them by complete LR(0) core, and inspect the resulting lookahead unions. State numbering has no semantic meaning by itself.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The C C grammar has canonical states that can be merged without introducing conflicts; the crossed A/B grammar shows why checking the resulting cells matters.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict says that the chosen parser construction cannot decide an action in that cell. An ambiguity claim additionally needs two parse trees for one complete word.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The assignment grammar has an SLR conflict but a conflict-free canonical LR(1) construction, so the SLR conflict alone was insufficient evidence of ambiguity.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Do not confuse one parser failure with a proof that no deterministic grammar for the language exists.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave canonical LR, LALR and lookahead, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: SLR adds a completed A production under every token in FOLLOW(A), even when some of those tokens cannot follow this item in its actual context. This approximation can create a conflict.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A shift/reduce or reduce/reduce conflict says that the chosen parser construction cannot decide an action in that cell. An ambiguity claim additionally needs two parse trees for one complete word.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Take a small example of find the limitation of global FOLLOW and work it out before looking at the explanation. Then compare your reasoning.

episodes.description: Evaluate dependencies and pass declaration context.
topics: Pass inherited context through a declaration

chapters.title: Pass inherited context through a declaration

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Maya and Leo here. Our section today is Attributes and syntax-directed translation.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: evaluate dependencies and pass declaration context.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with compute values with synthesized attributes and work our way to pass inherited context through a declaration.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Now for compute values with synthesized attributes. What's the key distinction?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A syntax-directed definition attaches attributes and equations to grammar productions. A synthesized attribute flows from children to their parent, so child values must be available first.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Attribute means information associated with a grammar-symbol occurrence.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For 2 + 3 * 4, the multiplication node synthesizes 12, then the addition node synthesizes 14.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The tree determines the dependencies.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We also need to talk about evaluate position and value attributes.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Give each binary digit a position inherited from its context, then synthesize its contribution as bit × 2^position. Sum the child contributions and apply the sign at the root only after the magnitude is known.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Inherited position means a digit’s context giving its power of two.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For -1011, the digit positions are 3, 2, 1 and 0; contributions are 8, 0, 2 and 1.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Their magnitude is 11 and the signed value is -11.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An inherited attribute supplies information from a parent or permitted sibling context. A declaration type can flow down to every identifier, while synthesized information flows back upward.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Inherited means information supplied from parent or permitted sibling context.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: In float alpha, beta;, the declaration supplies float to both identifiers before their symbol entries are recorded.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An arbitrary attribute dependency can be cyclic.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave attributes and syntax-directed translation, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A syntax-directed definition attaches attributes and equations to grammar productions. A synthesized attribute flows from children to their parent, so child values must be available first.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An inherited attribute supplies information from a parent or permitted sibling context. A declaration type can flow down to every identifier, while synthesized information flows back upward.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: You can pause here and try the Attributes and syntax-directed translation activities. Pick one idea and see whether you can explain it without the notes.

Represent expressions as trees, DAGs and IR

chapters.title: Source, assembly, object and machine code
Front end, intermediate form and back end
Represent expressions as trees, DAGs and IR

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, it's Maya. I've got Leo with me for Compiler pipeline and intermediate forms.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: connect source meaning to explicit intermediate operations.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with source, assembly, object and machine code and work our way to build three-address instructions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We also need to talk about source, assembly, object and machine code.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A source language describes the program for people and tools. Assembly names target operations symbolically; an assembler encodes them. A linker resolves references across object files and libraries.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Source means the program representation being translated.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A compiler may emit assembly or object code.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The object can still contain unresolved external references that linking must fix.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's start with front end, intermediate form and back end. What do we need to know?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The front end analyzes source rules and produces an intermediate representation. The back end lowers that representation for a target machine. Optimization can occur at several intermediate levels.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Intermediate representation means a structured form used between source analysis and target generation.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A new source language can reuse a target back end if both agree on a suitable intermediate form and its semantics.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Machine-independent does not mean semantics-free: types, side effects and evaluation rules still constrain transformations.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An expression tree records operator nesting. A DAG can share equivalent pure subexpressions when operands are unchanged. Linear IR names intermediate results so later passes can analyze dependencies.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Temporary means an intermediate result name, independent of a physical register.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For (2 + 3) * (2 + 3), a tree has two addition nodes; a DAG may share that pure sum.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The basic TAC emitter intentionally emits both before optimization.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Sharing is unsafe when repeated operations have observable side effects or changed operands.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A basic TAC operation assigns one operator result to a destination using at most two explicit operands. More complex expressions become a sequence whose temporary names expose dependencies.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Postfix means an operand-first representation with an operator after its arguments.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For 2 + 3 * 4, write t1 = 3 * 4 followed by t2 = 2 + t1.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: The temporary is an abstract name, not necessarily a physical register.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Three-address code does not mean every instruction literally has three operands; copies, branches and unary operations have different shapes.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave compiler pipeline and intermediate forms, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A source language describes the program for people and tools. Assembly names target operations symbolically; an assembler encodes them. A linker resolves references across object files and libraries.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A basic TAC operation assigns one operator result to a destination using at most two explicit operands. More complex expressions become a sequence whose temporary names expose dependencies.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A useful next step is to revisit build three-address instructions with an example of your own. Keep it small enough to check by hand.

chapters.title: Rename definitions with SSA and φ
Build basic blocks and a control-flow graph

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Welcome to CSQuest Audio. I'm Maya, here with Leo. This section is called SSA and control flow.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: follow definitions and edges through a program.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with rename definitions with SSA and φ and work our way to build basic blocks and a control-flow graph.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Let's start with rename definitions with SSA and φ. What do we need to know?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Static single assignment gives each named version exactly one static definition. At a control-flow join, a φ instruction chooses the version from the edge actually taken.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Definition means a point that assigns a value to a name.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: If B1 defines x1 = 2 and B2 defines x2 = 5, B3 can use x3 = φ(B1:x1, B2:x2).

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: It selects 2 or 5, never their sum.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Static single definition does not mean the instruction executes only once; a loop instruction can execute repeatedly at runtime.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to build basic blocks and a control-flow graph. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and an instruction following a control transfer. Each maximal basic block has one entry and transfers outside only at its end. CFG edges record possible successors.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Basic block means a maximal straight-line instruction sequence with one entry.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: A conditional branch has a target edge and a fall-through edge.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An unconditional goto has only its target; return exits.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: CFG here means control-flow graph, distinct from context-free grammar in parsing discussions.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave SSA and control flow, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Static single assignment gives each named version exactly one static definition. At a control-flow join, a φ instruction chooses the version from the edge actually taken.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Leaders are the first instruction, every jump target, and an instruction following a control transfer. Each maximal basic block has one entry and transfers outside only at its end. CFG edges record possible successors.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: We've covered a lot in SSA and control flow. You don't have to remember every detail at once; start by trying one of the examples yourself.

episodes.subject: cd
episodes.title: Optimization and data-flow analysis
episodes.description: Prove local changes safe with liveness and availability facts.
topics: Optimize only when behavior is preserved
Discover live variables before removing code
Check USE, DEF, IN and OUT separately
Find expressions available on every path

chapters.title: Optimize only when behavior is preserved
Discover live variables before removing code
Check USE, DEF, IN and OUT separately
Find expressions available on every path

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Hi, I'm Maya. Leo's with me, and today's section is called Optimization and data-flow analysis.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Here's what we're working toward: prove local changes safe with liveness and availability facts.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: We'll begin with optimize only when behavior is preserved and work our way to find expressions available on every path.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: That takes us to optimize only when behavior is preserved. Where does it fit?

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An optimization needs a semantic justification: fold known pure constants, reuse a common expression only while its operands remain unchanged, or remove a write whose value is never observed.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Pure operation means a computation with no observable side effect under the stated model.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: If t = a + b and u = a + b have no intervening operand changes or side effects, u can reuse t.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An unused call cannot be removed merely because its return value is ignored.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Side effects, aliasing, exceptions and floating-point behavior can invalidate arithmetic-looking rewrites.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: There's another piece to this: discover live variables before removing code.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A value is live at a point when some continuation may use it before the next definition. Liveness is a backward may analysis: successor facts combine by union, then the current definition kills an older value.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: USE means names whose current values are read by the instruction.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: For y = x + 1, x is used before the statement, and the old y is overwritten.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Return y makes the new y live afterward.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A loop back edge can send a future use back to an earlier point. Start with empty live sets and repeat backward transfer until no set changes, rather than assuming one pass suffices.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: DEF means names written by the instruction.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: A branch back to y = x + 1 can make x live around the loop even though the source text appears to have moved beyond its first use.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Union is essential: a value needed on one possible path is live even if another path does not use it.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: USE contains values read before a local definition; DEF contains names assigned. OUT joins successor IN sets, and IN adds USE while removing killed incoming values. Keep the four sets distinct.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Live value means a value some continuation may read before it is redefined.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: For x = x + 1, x belongs to both USE and DEF: its old value is read and a new value is written.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Removing DEF before adding USE prevents losing that read.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: I want to unpack find expressions available on every path next.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An expression is available when it has already been computed on every path to the point and none of its operands has been redefined. Availability is forward and combines predecessors with intersection.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: GEN means expressions computed and still valid at the end of a block.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: If one diamond branch rewrites a while the other preserves a + b, a + b is not available at the join; the two paths disagree.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Replacing intersection with the liveness union rule makes common-subexpression elimination unsafe.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: Before we leave optimization and data-flow analysis, let's connect the pieces.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: An optimization needs a semantic justification: fold known pure constants, reuse a common expression only while its operands remain unchanged, or remove a write whose value is never observed.

turns.speaker: leo
turns.text: An expression is available when it has already been computed on every path to the point and none of its operands has been redefined. Availability is forward and combines predecessors with intersection.

turns.speaker: maya
turns.text: Try explaining find expressions available on every path in your own words. If you get stuck, that chapter is a good place to listen again.
